finalText:
**Short answer:** 301 and 308 both mean "this resource has moved permanently." The difference is what the client may do with the method. After a 301, a client may turn a POST into a GET, which drops the request body. After a 308, it may not. Both are cacheable by default (the RFCs call it "heuristically cacheable"). Both are now defined in RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics, June 2022).

**What each means**

RFC 9110 uses the same wording for both. 301 "indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs" (Section 15.4.2). Section 15.4.9 says the same about 308. In both cases the server SHOULD send a `Location` header with the new URI, and the client MAY follow it automatically. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html

**Method and body handling**

- **General rule:** when a client follows a redirect automatically, it "SHOULD resend the original request message" to the new URI. It should also "Change the request method according to the redirecting status code's semantics, if applicable." If the method has been changed to GET or HEAD, the client removes content-specific headers such as Content-Type and Content-Length. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
- **301:** RFC 9110 says that "For historical reasons, a user agent MAY change the request method from POST to GET for the subsequent request". It adds that 308 can be used if that isn't wanted. When this happens, the POST body isn't sent on. (The spec only says the content headers are removed; I'm inferring that the body goes too, since a GET without those headers carries no content.) This exception exists because HTTP/1.0 originally defined 301 to keep the method. Browsers then split on what to do with POST, and "Prevailing practice eventually converged on changing the method to GET." The spec was later changed to allow this, and 307 and 308 "were later added to unambiguously indicate method-preserving redirects". https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
- **308:** the client must repeat the request with the same method and body. RFC 7538, which created 308, says it "is similar to 301 (Moved Permanently) ... except that it does not allow changing the request method from POST to GET." https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html

One thing to be aware of: RFC 9110's own 308 section doesn't repeat that "similar to 301" sentence. In RFC 9110, the rule that 308 keeps the method comes from the 3xx overview note and the note under 301 quoted above.

**Cacheability**

RFC 9110 says both "301 response" and "308 response" are "heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls". Section 15.1 lists 301 and 308 among the heuristically cacheable codes. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html

In practice, a cache can store and reuse either response without explicit freshness information by estimating an expiry time itself. A `Cache-Control` header or the method's definition can override that. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html

RFC 7538 calls 308 "cacheable by default" rather than "heuristically cacheable" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html). This isn't a real disagreement: RFC 9111 says the older specs called these status codes "cacheable by default" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html).

**Where each is specified**

- **301:** RFC 9110, Section 15.4.2. It was previously in RFC 7231, Section 6.4.2.
- **308:** RFC 9110, Section 15.4.9. It was first defined in RFC 7538 (April 2015), which replaced the earlier Experimental RFC 7238 "with no technical changes" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).
- **Status of the older RFCs:** RFC 9110's header lists "Obsoletes: 2818, 7230, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694". So RFC 7231 and RFC 7538 are both replaced. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
- **Caveat:** the text I got from RFC 7538's own page doesn't show an "Obsoleted by" line. The evidence for its replacement is RFC 9110's header.

RFC 9110 also warns that 308 "is much younger (June 2014) than its sibling codes and thus might not be recognized everywhere". It points to RFC 7538, Section 4, which suggests an HTML meta refresh as a fallback for clients that don't understand 308.

I didn't check MDN or any other secondary source, so this is based only on the RFCs.
